summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In an Oregon case, the court held city police officers who assisted an ORS 419B.150 removal at the direction of Oregon DHS were entitled to qualified immunity because their reliance on the agency's protective-custody determination was objectively reasonable.
key_cases.relevance: Construes ORS 419B.150 protective custody and the division of responsibility between DHS and assisting officers.
key_cases.quote: Sjurset correctly points out, however, that an officer cannot blindly rely on the existence of a protective-custody determination to avoid liability.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court held a genuine dispute existed as to whether a newborn was in imminent danger justifying warrantless removal, because social workers may not forgo a warrant if they had adequate time to obtain one without risking the child.
key_cases.relevance: Constrains emergency protective custody where the child is already under supervision and no immediate threat exists.
key_cases.quote: under Rogers, the social workers here lacked cause to forgo a warrant if they had adequate time to pursue one through the ordinary judicial process

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held a social worker was not entitled to summary judgment on a warrantless-seizure claim because officials must obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child absent reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the federal constitutional floor for emergency protective custody in the circuit that governs Oregon.
key_cases.quote: Government officials are required to obtain prior judicial authorization before intruding on a parent's custody of her child unless they possess information at the time of the seizure

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. M. P.
key_cases.holding: The court held a protective custody order under ORS 419B.150 is not an 'initial child custody determination' and the supporting declaration is not the first pleading, so the dependency proceeding commenced when the petition was filed, defeating UCCJEA home-state jurisdiction.
key_cases.relevance: This is the most detailed recent Oregon appellate account of the ORS 419B.150 protective custody mechanism and its legal effect.
key_cases.quote: An issued but unexecuted protective custody order does not trigger the juvenile court's jurisdiction or commence any time period during which a petition must be filed.

reporting_details: Oregon is not a universal-reporting state: only the “public or private officials” listed in Or. Rev. Stat. § 419B.005(6) must immediately report suspected child abuse, and they report through the centralized Oregon Child Abuse Hotline or to a local law enforcement agency (Or. Rev. Stat. §§ 419B.010(1), 419B.015(1)(a)); the duty is personal to the official regardless of any employer’s internal reporting policy (§ 419B.010(3), (4)), privileged communications to a psychiatrist, psychologist, member of the clergy, attorney or guardian ad litem are excepted (§ 419B.010(1)), failure to report is a Class A violation (§ 419B.010(5)), and any other person may report voluntarily (§ 419B.015(1)(a)).
